Session 5 · 5.1 Authentication versus authorizationBook ↗

Two questions

  • Authentication: "Who are you?" Password, phone code, fingerprint, Google login
  • Authorization: "What may you do?" May Dana see order 90? Sam's order 88? Issue a refund?
  • Office building: the badge check is authentication; which doors open is authorization
  • Authorization is organised by roles: customer, staff, manager, administrator
Every request touching a record must check that THIS user may touch THIS record. Forgetting that has caused huge leaks.
Session 5 · 5.2 Passwords done rightBook ↗

Never store the password

  • Store a hash: a one-way scramble that cannot be reversed. Check a login by hashing what was typed
  • A stolen database then reveals no passwords. (Salted, with slow algorithms such as bcrypt)
  • If a company can email you your old password, it is doing this wrong
  • Multi-factor authentication: something you know + something you have (or are). Require it for staff
  • Passkeys: a device-held key unlocked by fingerprint or face; no password at all
Session 5 · 5.3 Staying logged in: cookies, sessions, tokens · 1/2Book ↗

How a login survives stateless HTTP

  • The password is sent once. A random session ID in a cookie stands in for it afterwards
  • Any web server in the pool looks the ID up in the shared session store
Session 5 · 5.3 Staying logged in: cookies, sessions, tokens · 2/2Book ↗

Consequences

  • The cookie is as good as the password while it lasts: HTTPS-only, invisible to JavaScript, re-ask for sensitive actions
  • This is exactly what lets stateless, load-balanced servers work
  • The same mechanism lets advertisers track browsers across sites: hence consent banners
  • Apps and APIs often use a signed token (a JSON Web Token) sent in a header instead of a cookie
Session 5 · 5.4 HTTP Basic Authentication and API keys · 1/2Book ↗

The simplest scheme, built into HTTP

  • Basic Auth sends username:password on every request, encoded in Base64, which anyone can decode
  • Only over HTTPS; only for staging sites, internal tools, and some APIs
Session 5 · 5.4 HTTP Basic Authentication and API keys · 2/2Book ↗

API keys are passwords for programs

  • A long random secret a provider issues so it knows whom to bill
  • Stored in server configuration (environment variables, a .env file); never in front-end code; never in Git
  • Bots scan GitHub constantly for leaked keys and can spend thousands within minutes
The single most important habit when building with Claude Code and the Claude API.
Session 5 · 5.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works · 1/3Book ↗

The problem OAuth solves

  • New apps want login without another password; apps want to use your Google Calendar or bank on your behalf
  • Typing your Google password into a third-party app would give it everything, forever
  • OAuth 2.0: the user approves a limited request at the trusted service; the app gets a valet key
  • Four roles: resource owner (you), client (the app), authorization server (Google login), resource server (Google's API)
Session 5 · 5.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works · 2/3Book ↗

The authorization-code flow

Session 5 · 5.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works · 3/3Book ↗

Why the roundabout design

  • The password is typed only at Google; the app never sees it
  • Scopes limit what the access token can do; the user sees them on the consent screen
  • The one-time code is swapped for the token server-to-server, using the app's client secret
  • Tokens expire in about an hour; the user can revoke any app with one click
  • OpenID Connect adds an ID token for login; single sign-on lets employees use one company identity everywhere
Offer "Sign in with Google": higher conversion, no password liability. And always read the scopes.
Session 5 · 5.6 Security basics every product owner should knowBook ↗

Six ideas that catch most mistakes

  • Encrypt in transit (HTTPS) and at rest (encrypted disks)
  • Never trust the front end: prices, permissions, secrets live on the server
  • SQL injection: user text pasted into a query. Typing ' OR 1=1 -- logs in as everyone. Frameworks prevent it with parameterised queries
  • Least privilege: every person, program, and key gets the minimum access
  • Secrets out of code and out of Git; rotate anything exposed
  • Patch software and test that backups restore
"Have we reviewed against the OWASP Top Ten?" is a question any engineer or AI assistant can act on.

Session 5 · 5.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded · 2/3Book ↗

One back end, many clients

  • Different front ends are different faces on the same product; the API and database do not change
Session 5 · 5.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded · 3/3Book ↗

What this explains

  • "We need an app" is a new front end if the API exists, and secretly a back-end project if it does not
  • Companies start with the web: no store review, no commission, one codebase, instant updates
  • The API outlives several generations of front ends
  • Embedded devices are the exception: a 2026 thermostat must work in 2036; a mistake is a recall, not a redeploy
Session 5 · 5.8 Where AI fits · 1/2Book ↗

An AI model is a third-party API called from your back end

  • The key and the model call stay on the server; the browser talks only to your back end
Session 5 · 5.8 Where AI fits · 2/2Book ↗

Three practical consequences

  • The API key stays on the server: a call from the browser exposes it to every visitor
  • Your data is the differentiator: add this customer's history and your catalogue to the prompt (RAG)
  • AI calls cost money per token, take seconds, and can fail: cache, monitor, and give them a fallback
Claude itself is served through exactly this architecture. Now you know what is on the other end of the request.
